domain_label: Sweater Vertical — AI-Design Sizing and Grading Math for the 3-Article California Knitwear Line
purpose: An exact, knit-specific method for the AI-design owner to size and grade the 3-article D2C line (A1 cotton-blend 12GG core, A2 fine-acrylic 7-12GG value/youth, A3 thin merino/lambswool premium) by specifying FINISHED-garment (not body) measurements across the US XS-XXL set with ~5-6 inch ease, fixing the four knit measurements (chest, body length, sleeve length, hem) plus an M base in inches, applying the linear grade rule (chest +2 in/size, body +1.5, sleeve +0.75, hem +2; full-chest 38->48 across XS->XXL), translating those inches into whole wales/courses at the production gauge, setting a post-wash target with a per-fibre shrinkage allowance and a tolerance at every measurement point, and closing the loop with the Turlock pop-up fitting lab that sets the real production size curve.
assumptions: no proprietary per-construction stitch-density or shrinkage dataset is supplied; gauge-to-stitch conversions, ease bands, and per-fibre shrink allowances are reasoned estimates keyed to the design deep-dive and yarn/machines files, not a measured PPS swatch

the line is the 3-article fibre/role ladder fixed upstream (A1 cotton-blend core, A2 fine-acrylic value/youth, A3 merino/lambswool premium), all fine-gauge ~12GG for the warm-California weight, gender-neutral soft-boxy fit
the size set is the US XS-S-M-L-XL-XXL unisex men's-derived block published with a size-up/size-down note, fitted from a washed relaxed swatch to a post-wash target
the tech-pack spec is FINISHED-garment flat/half measurements in inches, never body measurements; body charts are a downstream sanity check only

any price, MOQ, CAC, duty, or throughput figure is a labeled estimate band tagged estimate-not-actual with method and confidence, never a faked precise number, and US sweater duties are cotton 6110.20.20 ~16.5 percent, wool 6110.11 ~16 percent, acrylic/MMF 6110.30.30 ~32 percent
the production size curve (the XS:S:M:L:XL:XXL ratio) is UNKNOWN until the Turlock pop-ups run and is treated as a launch hypothesis the fitting lab validates or breaks
exclusions: silhouette, stitch-palette, colour, and detail design judgement (the texture-over-colour design decisions handled in the design deep-dive sec 1-2)
the Flux generative prompt method, eight-slot skeleton, parameters, and image-to-spec bridge (handled in the design deep-dive sec 5-7 and a separate KB)
trend ingestion, the drop calendar, and the Central-Valley-youth hype listening loop (design deep-dive sec 4)
yarn fibre/count selection, dye-lot MOQ, and the anti-pill contractual spec (the yarn specialist KB), referenced here only where shrinkage and spirality bear on dimension
machine selection, the CAD programmer authoring the needle-action program, and linker throughput (the machines specialist KB), referenced here only as the inch-to-stitch translation hand-off
landed-cost, pricing, and unit-economics modeling (the logistics specialist KB); article price bands appear only as positioning context
source_description: reasoned estimate priors for sizing and grading work units, grounded in the AI Design Specialist deep-dive (DEEPDIVE.md sec 3 sizing+grading math, sec 7 image-to-spec bridge), the SCOPE_GLOSSARY knitting and finishing vocabulary (gauge/GG, wales/courses, stitch density, loop length, shrinkage/spirality, milling, sanforising, tolerance, tech pack), the yarn deep-dive (fibre tier ladder, per-fibre shrink behaviour, balanced-ply spirality control), the machines deep-dive (the CAD programmer translating the inch-grade into whole wales/courses as the scarce bottleneck), and the brand_market deep-dive (the ~24 percent online vs ~6 percent in-store return gap, size as the #1 apparel return reason, the pop-ups as the size-curve link); no supplied measurement dataset

competency_questions.question: Why must the tech-pack carry FINISHED-garment measurements rather than body measurements, and what error does confusing the two ship?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: FINISHED_VS_BODY states the spec is finished flat/half-garment in inches, that body chest plus ease equals garment chest with ~4-6 inch sweater ease at the upper ~5-6 inch end for the soft-boxy fit, and that confusing the two ships a sweater a full size off

competency_questions.question: What is the US size set and unisex block the line is graded on, and how is it published to the buyer?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SIZE_SET_BLOCK names the XS-S-M-L-XL-XXL six-size set on a unisex men's-derived block published with a size-down-for-fitted / true-to-size-for-oversized note

competency_questions.question: What are the four knit measurements the spec and QC turn on, and what is the M base in inches for each?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: FOUR_MEASUREMENTS_M_BASE names chest (42 in full / 21 flat), body length (28 in), sleeve length (35.5 in), and bottom hem width (20 in flat) at M plus the working secondaries

competency_questions.question: What is the linear grade rule across XS-XXL, and what is the resulting full-chest run?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: LINEAR_GRADE_RULE gives chest +2 in/size, body +1.5, sleeve +0.75, hem +2 (shoulder +0.5), uniform per size, yielding full-chest 38-40-42-44-46-48 across XS->XXL

competency_questions.question: How is any size's measurement computed from the M base, the grade increment, and the size index, so the full grade table regenerates exactly?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: GRADE_FORMULA defines measurement(size) = M_base + grade_increment x (size_index - M_index) with the integer size index XS=-2..XXL=+3 relative to M and recomputes at least the chest run as a worked check

competency_questions.question: How is an inch dimension translated into a whole number of wales and courses at the production gauge before it is programmable?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: INCH_TO_STITCH converts inches to wales/courses using the finished wales-per-inch and courses-per-inch at the GG, requires rounding every graded dimension to an integer stitch count, and hands the integer grade to the CAD programmer

competency_questions.question: How is the post-wash finished target set so the garment lands on-spec after relaxation, and how does the allowance differ per fibre?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: POST_WASH_TARGET specifies building to a post-wash target with <=3-5 percent residual shrinkage in the PO and a per-fibre knit-larger allowance: cotton (A1) shrinks/bags most, merino (A3) mills/relaxes, acrylic (A2) is dimensionally stable but heat-sensitive

competency_questions.question: Why must a tolerance be set at every measurement point, and what happens without one?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: TOLERANCE_GATE sets per-point tolerances (e.g. chest +/-0.5 in, length +/-0.75, sleeve +/-0.5), makes out-of-tolerance a reject, and states that without tolerances the grade rule is decorative

competency_questions.question: How does the gauge<->grade<->shrinkage interaction couple, so a change in one ripples to the others?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: GAUGE_GRADE_SHRINK_INTERACTION shows the chain: gauge sets the inch<->stitch conversion, the integer-wale rounding constrains the grade, loop length tunes density to hit GSM and dimension together, and the post-wash target plus per-fibre allowance close it on a washed swatch

competency_questions.question: How does spirality threaten the graded dimension, and what spinning-side control kills it?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SPIRALITY_CONTROL names the twisted-side-seam defect from unbalanced singles twist, requires balanced ply in the yarn PO, and ties it to dimensional stability of the graded panel

competency_questions.question: How is the size grade and ease validated against the local Central-Valley body, rather than assumed from the national chart?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: LOCAL_BODY_VALIDATION states the linear grade and 5-6 inch ease are launch hypotheses validated or broken against the ~46 percent-Hispanic Central-Valley population at the pop-ups, with a possible non-linear break at XS/XXL

competency_questions.question: How do the Turlock pop-ups capture the production size curve, and why is a wrong curve costly?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: POPUP_FITTING_LAB records the size bought (and ideally measured chest) per fitted customer so the distribution of sizes sold becomes the XS:S:M:L:XL:XXL production ratio, and states a wrong curve means dead stock in the tails plus stock-outs in the middle plus markdown

competency_questions.question: How does the offline fitting lab buy down the online return rate, and how is the size guide calibrated?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: RETURN_REDUCTION cites the ~24 percent online vs ~6 percent in-store return gap and size as the #1 apparel return reason, and routes each offline fitting into a calibrated online size guide

competency_questions.question: On what cadence and triggers is the size system re-run, and how are its numeric claims labeled honestly?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: GRADE_REVIEW_LOOP sets a per-drop pop-up-curve-to-grade review with triggers (return spike, curve drift, swatch shrink change), and HONESTY_LABELING tags every ease/density/shrink/return figure estimate-not-actual with a confirmation path

glossary.definition: A flat/half measurement of the made-up sweater laid out, doubled where noted to a full circumference, specified in inches on the tech pack; it equals body measurement plus ease and is what knit QC and fit turn on, never the wearer's body dimension.

The added inches between the body and the finished garment; sweaters carry ~4-6 inches of layering ease and this soft-boxy unisex line sits at the upper ~5-6 inch end, so finished chest at M (body ~38 in) lands ~42-43 in full.

An even grade that applies one fixed increment per measurement uniformly across every size step (chest +2 in/size, body +1.5, sleeve +0.75, hem +2), as opposed to a non-linear grade that breaks the increment at the size extremes; the launch default until pop-up returns justify a break.

A wale is a column of loops running up the fabric (width direction, set by needles/gauge); a course is a row of loops running across (length direction, set by knitting rows). A sweater is knit to a whole number of wales and courses, so an inch grade is only valid once it lands on an integer count at the production density.

Loops per unit length and width (wales per inch x courses per inch) at the finished, relaxed state; it pairs with GG and yarn count to fix GSM and is the lever, via loop length, that the programmer tunes to hit weight and dimension simultaneously.

The finished dimension specified AFTER relaxation/steaming and at least one home wash; the garment is knit slightly larger so it lands on-spec once it relaxes and shrinks, with a residual-shrinkage cap (e.g. <=3-5 percent) written into the PO.

The knit-larger margin that differs by fibre even though the inch-grade is shared: cotton (A1) shrinks most and bags out, merino (A3) mills and relaxes, acrylic (A2) is dimensionally stable but heat-sensitive and cannot be hard-pressed.

The plus/minus band allowed at each measurement point (e.g. chest +/-0.5 in, length +/-0.75, sleeve +/-0.5); a garment outside tolerance is a reject, and without a tolerance at every point the grade rule is decorative.

The twisted-side-seam defect in which the side seam spirals around the body, caused by unbalanced singles twist; killed by requiring balanced ply in the yarn PO, it is a dimensional-stability failure that distorts the graded panel.

The XS:S:M:L:XL:XXL ratio to manufacture, read off the distribution of sizes actually sold at the Turlock pop-ups; UNKNOWN until the pop-ups run, and a wrong curve produces dead stock in the tails, stock-outs in the middle, and markdown.
The integer offset of a size from the M base used by the grade formula (XS=-2, S=-1, M=0, L=+1, XL=+2, XXL=+3), so any size's measurement is M_base plus grade_increment times the size index.

nodes.definition: Fix the foundational rule that the tech-pack spec is FINISHED-garment flat/half measurements in inches, never body measurements: body chest plus ease equals garment chest, sweaters carry ~4-6 inches of layering ease, and this soft-boxy unisex line sits at the upper ~5-6 inch end. Grade the garment and only then sanity-check against published body charts. Confusing the two is the #1 sizing error and ships a sweater a full size off. This rule bounds every measurement, grade, and tolerance decision downstream.

included: the finished-vs-body distinction
the ~4-6 inch (upper ~5-6) ease band
the full-size-off failure of confusing them

pros.claim: Anchoring the whole spec to finished-garment inches removes the single most common sizing mistake before any number is set
pros.example: specifying finished chest 42 in at M (body ~38 in plus ~4-5 in ease) instead of writing body 38 and shipping a sweater a size too small

cons.claim: A pure finished-garment spec without a body-chart cross-check can drift from any real wearer if the ease assumption is wrong
cons.example: a finished spec built on ~6 in ease that reads as a tent on the local body the pop-ups later reveal runs slimmer

failure_modes: writing body measurements on the tech pack so the factory adds ease again or none at all
treating the ease band as fixed when the fit intent is fitted rather than soft-boxy
acceptance_tests: the spec states finished flat/half measurements in inches, names the ~4-6 inch ease band at the upper ~5-6 inch end, and flags that confusing finished with body ships a full size off
revisit_triggers: the fit intent changes from soft-boxy to fitted or cropped
pop-up data shows the ease assumption is off for the local body

base.update_signal: the fit intent or the validated ease band changes

nodes.definition: Establish the size set and base block the line is graded on: the US six-size run XS-S-M-L-XL-XXL on a unisex men's-derived block (broader, straighter than a women's block), published to the buyer with an explicit 'size down for a fitted look, true-to-size for oversized' note so the gender-neutral soft-boxy fit reads correctly. The unisex block widens the addressable buyer per MOQ-expensive SKU (3 styles x ~3 colours x 6 sizes = 54 SKUs already), which is why exactly one block is graded rather than separate men's and women's curves.

included: the XS-XXL six-size set
the unisex men's-derived block
the published size-up/size-down note

pros.claim: One unisex block across six sizes maximizes the addressable buyer per SKU while keeping the SKU count survivable against dye-lot MOQ
pros.example: publishing a single XS-XXL unisex grade so a 54-SKU capsule serves both men and women instead of doubling into separate blocks

cons.claim: A unisex block fits neither a markedly narrow nor a markedly broad body perfectly and leans on the buyer reading the fit note
cons.example: a customer expecting a women's-cut fit ordering true-to-size and finding the soft-boxy unisex cut roomier than wanted

failure_modes: publishing the size set with no fit-intent note so buyers self-select the wrong size
splitting into separate men's/women's blocks and breaking the SKU/MOQ ceiling
acceptance_tests: the XS-S-M-L-XL-XXL set and the unisex men's-derived block are named with the published size-up/size-down fit note
revisit_triggers: the addressable buyer or fit intent shifts toward a gendered cut
the pop-up curve shows a size in the set is never sold and could be dropped

base.update_signal: the size set, block, or fit-intent note changes

nodes.definition: Pin the four finished measurements knit QC and fit turn on, with the M base in inches: chest (half flat, 21 in; full 42 in), body length HPS-to-hem (28 in), sleeve length shoulder-to-cuff (35.5 in), and bottom hem width (half flat, 20 in), plus the working secondaries at M (shoulder ~18.5 in, armhole depth ~10 in, cuff rib ~3.5 in, hem rib ~2.5-3 in). These four points are the load that the grade rule, the inch-to-stitch translation, the post-wash target, and the tolerance gate all operate on; the crop variant runs body length -2 in.

included: the four finished measurements and their M-base inches
the working secondaries at M
the crop-variant length offset
excluded: how the values grade across sizes

pros.claim: Fixing four measurements plus an M base gives the grade, QC, and translation a small exact spine instead of a vague midweight description
pros.example: specifying finished chest 42 in, body 28 in, sleeve 35.5 in, hem 20 in at M as the four numbers every downstream step grades from

cons.claim: Four primary points can miss a fit problem living in an ungraded secondary like armhole depth or neck width
cons.example: a correct chest and length but a too-shallow armhole on the dropped-shoulder cut that the four-point spec did not catch

failure_modes: specifying only chest and length and leaving sleeve or hem to the factory
mixing half-flat and full-circumference values without labeling which is which
acceptance_tests: chest (21 flat/42 full), body length 28, sleeve 35.5, and hem 20 flat are stated at M with the working secondaries and the crop offset
revisit_triggers: the fit block or silhouette variant changes a base measurement
a pop-up fitting reveals a needed secondary measurement

base.update_signal: an M-base measurement or a tracked secondary changes

nodes.definition: Set the linear (even) grade applied uniformly across XS-XXL: chest +2 in/size, body length +1.5, sleeve length +0.75, hem width +2 (tracking chest to hold the straight silhouette), and shoulder +0.5, each increment industry-standard for knitwear. The full-chest run is 38-40-42-44-46-48 across XS->XXL, cross-checked against published US sweater charts. Launch linear and let pop-up returns prove whether a non-linear break is warranted at the XS/XXL extremes rather than pre-engineering complexity the data has not justified.

included: the per-measurement linear increments
the full-chest 38-48 run
the linear-first launch policy

pros.claim: A single uniform increment per measurement is the simplest defensible grade and the easiest to translate to stitches and audit in QC
pros.example: applying +2 in chest per step to land 38-40-42-44-46-48 full-chest, a clean run any factory can hit and any inspector can check

cons.claim: A purely linear grade can fit the tails worse than the middle if the local body needs a smaller XS step or a larger XXL step
cons.example: an XXL buyer finding the +2 in chest step too tight because the real population needs a non-linear break the linear launch did not include

failure_modes: pre-engineering a non-linear grade before any return data justifies it
applying an increment inconsistently so the run is no longer even
acceptance_tests: the increments chest +2 / body +1.5 / sleeve +0.75 / hem +2 (shoulder +0.5) are stated and yield full-chest 38-40-42-44-46-48
revisit_triggers: pop-up returns show a fit break at XS or XXL
the validated grade increment changes for the local body

base.update_signal: a grade increment or the linear-vs-nonlinear policy changes

nodes.definition: Define the formula that computes any size's measurement from the M base, the grade increment, and the size index, so the full grade table regenerates exactly and recomputes on any base or increment change: measurement(size) = M_base + grade_increment x (size_index - M_index), with the integer size index XS=-2, S=-1, M=0, L=+1, XL=+2, XXL=+3 (M_index=0). Worked check on full chest (M_base=42, increment=+2): XS=42+2x(-2)=38, S=40, M=42, L=44, XL=46, XXL=48 — matching the LINEAR_GRADE_RULE run. The same formula runs body (28, +1.5 -> 25.0/26.5/28/29.5/31/32.5), sleeve (35.5, +0.75 -> 34.0/34.75/35.5/36.25/37.0/37.75), and hem (20, +1.0 half / +2 full). This node is the recomputing engine of the KB.

included: the measurement(size) recompute formula
the integer size-index definition
the worked chest/body/sleeve/hem checks
excluded: the post-wash shrink offset applied after

pros.claim: One formula keyed to the size index regenerates the entire grade table exactly and lets a base or increment edit propagate without hand-editing every cell
pros.example: changing the chest increment to +1.75 and re-running measurement(size) to regenerate all six chest values in one pass

cons.claim: A single linear formula cannot express a non-linear grade break without adding a per-size correction term
cons.example: needing a +0.5 in correction only at XXL that the bare M_base + increment x index form cannot carry until extended

failure_modes: off-by-one in the size index so M is not zero and every size shifts
applying the formula to a half measurement while reporting a full circumference
acceptance_tests: the formula measurement(size)=M_base+increment x (size_index-M_index) is stated with the XS=-2..XXL=+3 index and recomputes full-chest to 38-40-42-44-46-48
revisit_triggers: a non-linear grade break requires a correction term added to the formula
the M base or any increment changes and the table must regenerate

base.update_signal: the grade formula or its size-index basis changes

nodes.definition: Characterize the production gauge and stitch density that set the inch<->stitch conversion: the line runs fine ~12GG for the warm-California elevated-basic weight, and the finished, relaxed fabric has a wales-per-inch and courses-per-inch density (illustratively ~9 wales/in finished) that must be measured on a physical PPS swatch, never assumed from the GG label alone. Stitch density (wales x courses per inch) pairs with GG and yarn count to fix GSM, and is the property that makes a graded inch land on a whole number of loops. The exact density at the line's construction is UNKNOWN until PPS sampling.

included: the ~12GG fine gauge and finished wales/courses density
the PPS-swatch measurement requirement
density pairing with GG and count to fix GSM
excluded: the rounding of a graded inch to stitches

pros.claim: Measuring real finished density on a swatch turns the abstract GG into the exact wales/courses-per-inch the grade must round to
pros.example: measuring ~9 wales/in on the washed swatch so a 2 in chest step is known to be ~18 wales rather than guessed

cons.claim: Density read off a single swatch can mislead if the bulk run knits at a different tension than the sample
cons.example: a sample swatch at 9 wales/in but a looser bulk run at 8.5 that shifts every stitch count

failure_modes: assuming a density from the GG label instead of measuring the swatch
measuring density under tension off-machine instead of relaxed
acceptance_tests: the ~12GG gauge and a measured (or explicitly UNKNOWN-until-PPS) finished wales/courses-per-inch density are stated as the inch-to-stitch basis
revisit_triggers: a PPS swatch measures a density different from the working assumption
the gauge or construction tension changes between sample and bulk

base.update_signal: the measured finished stitch density or the gauge changes

nodes.definition: Translate every graded inch dimension into a whole number of wales (width) and courses (length) at the production density before it is programmable, because a sweater is knit to a stitch/row count, not cut to a pattern. Multiply each graded width by finished wales-per-inch and each graded length by courses-per-inch, then round to the nearest integer stitch count; a +2 in chest grade is only valid if it lands on an integer number of wales per panel side (illustratively +2 in x ~9 wales/in = ~18 wales). The integer stitch grade, not the inch grade, is the artifact handed to the CAD/flat-knit programmer who authors the needle actions.

included: inch-to-wales/courses conversion and integer rounding
the per-panel-side validity check on the grade
the integer-grade hand-off to the programmer

pros.claim: Converting the inch-grade to whole wales and courses makes it actually programmable and exposes a grade that does not land on integer stitches
pros.example: rounding +2 in chest to +18 wales per side so the programmer can author it, instead of handing over a fractional-stitch grade no machine can knit

cons.claim: Rounding each dimension to integer stitches introduces small inch errors that can accumulate across many graded points
cons.example: rounding several dimensions up by a fraction of a wale so a panel reads slightly wide of the inch spec

failure_modes: handing the programmer an inch-grade that does not resolve to integer stitches
rounding so the accumulated error pushes a dimension out of tolerance
acceptance_tests: each graded dimension is converted to integer wales/courses at the production density and the integer stitch grade is the artifact handed to the programmer
revisit_triggers: the measured density changes the wales/courses per inch
rounding error pushes a graded dimension toward a tolerance edge

base.update_signal: the density-driven inch-to-stitch conversion or the rounding rule changes

nodes.definition: Specify finished dimensions as a POST-WASH target measured on a washed, relaxed swatch, with the garment knit slightly larger so it lands on-spec after relaxation/steaming and a home wash, and a residual-shrinkage cap (<=3-5 percent) written into the PO. Off-machine fabric is under tension and reads narrow and long, so a spec taken off-machine ships the wrong size; loop length and stitch density are tuned to hit GSM and the post-wash dimension simultaneously. This is the offset applied on top of the integer stitch grade, and it differs per fibre (PER_FIBRE_SHRINKAGE).

included: the post-wash, washed-swatch target
the knit-larger offset and <=3-5 percent residual cap
loop-length/density tuning to hit GSM and dimension
excluded: the tolerance band around the target

pros.claim: Building to a washed-swatch post-wash target lands the garment on-spec in the customer's hands instead of on the knitting bed
pros.example: knitting a panel ~3 percent larger so it relaxes and washes down to the 42 in finished chest rather than measuring 42 under tension and arriving small

cons.claim: A post-wash target depends on a wash-test swatch that takes time and can differ from the customer's actual laundering
cons.example: a swatch washed cool landing on target while a customer's hot wash shrinks the garment past the residual cap

failure_modes: specifying dimensions off-machine under tension so the washed garment lands small
omitting the residual-shrinkage cap from the PO so shrink is uncontrolled
acceptance_tests: finished dimensions are specified as a post-wash target on a washed swatch with a knit-larger offset and a <=3-5 percent residual-shrinkage cap in the PO
revisit_triggers: a wash-test swatch shows residual shrinkage outside the cap
the finishing route (milling, compacting, steaming) changes the relaxation behaviour

base.update_signal: the post-wash target, knit-larger offset, or residual cap changes

nodes.definition: Set the per-fibre knit-larger allowance that differs across the 3 articles even though the inch-grade is shared: cotton (A1) shrinks most and bags out, so its rib hems are hard and compacting/sanforising should be considered; merino (A3) mills and relaxes more, so milling is part of its finished dimension; acrylic (A2) is dimensionally stable but heat-sensitive and cannot be hard-pressed, so its allowance is small but its finishing temperature is capped. The grade table is one, but each article carries its own post-wash offset and finishing route to land that grade.

included: the per-article (A1 cotton / A2 acrylic / A3 merino) shrink/relax behaviour
the article-specific finishing route (compact, mill, low-heat)
one shared grade with per-fibre offsets

pros.claim: A per-fibre allowance lets one grade table serve all three articles while each lands on-spec given its own shrink behaviour
pros.example: knitting the A1 cotton core with a larger offset and a compacting step while the A2 acrylic carries a small offset and a temperature cap

cons.claim: Maintaining a distinct offset and finishing route per fibre adds sampling and QC overhead versus a single allowance
cons.example: running three wash-test swatches and three finishing routes for one capsule instead of one

failure_modes: applying the cotton allowance to acrylic and over-sizing the stable fibre
hard-pressing acrylic and glazing or distorting the heat-sensitive panel
acceptance_tests: each article has a stated shrink/relax behaviour and a matching finishing route and offset so the shared grade lands on-spec per fibre
revisit_triggers: a per-article wash-test swatch shows a different shrink than assumed
a fibre blend ratio change alters the shrink behaviour

base.update_signal: a per-fibre shrink behaviour or finishing route changes

nodes.definition: Set a plus/minus tolerance at every measurement point so the grade is enforceable: e.g. chest +/-0.5 in, body length +/-0.75, sleeve +/-0.5, with tighter bands on the points fit turns on and looser on secondaries. A garment outside tolerance at any point is a reject under the AQL sampling plan. Without a tolerance at every point the grade rule is decorative, because a factory hitting the nominal on average while drifting wide on individual garments still ships off-size product. The tolerance is measured against the post-wash target, not the off-machine dimension.

included: per-point +/- tolerance bands
out-of-tolerance as an AQL reject
tolerance measured against the post-wash target
excluded: the AQL sampling plan mechanics from QC

pros.claim: A tolerance at every point turns the grade from an average into an enforceable accept/reject contract
pros.example: rejecting a lot whose chest measures 43.2 in against a 42 +/-0.5 post-wash target even though the lot average is on nominal

cons.claim: Tolerances set too tight for the construction's natural variation drive false rejects and cost on an inherently variable knit
cons.example: a +/-0.25 in chest band rejecting good fully-fashioned panels whose relaxed width naturally varies more than that

failure_modes: specifying a grade with no tolerance so on-average is accepted as on-spec
setting a tolerance against the off-machine rather than the post-wash dimension
acceptance_tests: each measurement point carries a +/- tolerance against the post-wash target, with out-of-tolerance defined as a reject
revisit_triggers: false-reject rate shows the tolerance is mis-set for the construction
a fit complaint pattern shows a point needs a tighter tolerance

base.update_signal: a tolerance band or the reject rule changes

nodes.definition: Make explicit the knit-specific three-way coupling that is unique to knitwear: gauge sets the inch<->stitch conversion, the integer-wale rounding constrains which inch grades are even achievable, loop length and stitch density are the lever the programmer tunes to hit GSM and the dimension together, and the post-wash target plus per-fibre allowance close the loop on a washed swatch. A change in any one ripples to the others: finer gauge changes the wales-per-inch and therefore the stitch grade; a tighter density changes both GSM and shrink; a different fibre changes the knit-larger offset. This node is the integrating view the consolidated spec rests on.

included: the gauge<->grade<->shrinkage coupling and its ripple
loop length as the GSM-and-dimension lever
the swatch as the closing ground truth
excluded: the individual conversion, target, and per-fibre steps already specified

pros.claim: Treating gauge, grade, and shrinkage as one coupled system prevents fixing one number and silently breaking another

nodes.definition: Protect the graded dimension from spirality, the twisted-side-seam defect in which the side seam spirals around the body, caused by unbalanced singles twist that biases the fabric. Require balanced ply in the yarn PO (the twist dial that pairs opposing S/Z twists), because a panel knit to the correct integer stitch grade still ships off-spec and visually defective if it torques after washing. Spirality is a dimensional-stability failure alongside shrinkage, so it is gated in the same acceptance set and is most acute on fine singles-leaning fashion constructions.

included: spirality as a graded-dimension risk
balanced-ply requirement in the yarn PO
spirality gated with shrinkage in acceptance
excluded: the full yarn twist/ply spec owned by the yarn KB

pros.claim: Requiring balanced ply kills the twist that would distort an otherwise correctly graded panel after wash
pros.example: specifying balanced ply so the A1 cotton side seam stays straight instead of spiraling and reading as an off-size defect

cons.claim: Balanced ply and the associated twist control can raise yarn cost or limit the singles-light hand a fine fashion knit wants
cons.example: paying a ply premium that trims the lightness the 12GG elevated-basic look depends on

failure_modes: leaving twist/ply blank in the PO so unbalanced singles spiral the seam
treating spirality as a knit defect when it originates at the yarn twist
acceptance_tests: balanced ply is required in the yarn PO and spirality is gated with shrinkage as a dimensional-stability acceptance test
revisit_triggers: a wash test shows seam spiraling beyond the acceptance band
a yarn twist or ply change affects dimensional stability

base.update_signal: the spirality behaviour or the balanced-ply requirement changes

nodes.definition: Run the Turlock pop-ups as a fitting lab, not just a sales channel: per fitted customer, record the size bought and ideally the measured chest, turning each in-person try-on into a data point that calibrates the grade, the ease, and the online size guide. The pop-ups are the highest-value sizing input the brand owns because they observe the real local body and the real size chosen, which a national chart cannot. This is the offline instrument that both sets the production size curve and buys down the online return rate, looped every drop.

included: recording size-bought and measured chest per fitting
the pop-up as a fit/grade/size-guide calibration instrument
the per-drop loop

pros.claim: An in-person fitting lab observes the real local body and the real size chosen, the one input no national chart provides
pros.example: logging that local L buyers consistently chose M, signaling the ease runs roomy for the Central-Valley body before bulk commits

cons.claim: Pop-up samples are small, self-selected, and local, so the curve they yield can be biased toward early adopters
cons.example: a CSU-heavy pop-up over-weighting younger sizes that the broader ship-to-California shopper does not match

failure_modes: selling at pop-ups without recording size and fit so the data is lost
treating a tiny early sample as a final curve and over-committing production
acceptance_tests: the pop-up records size-bought (and ideally measured chest) per fitted customer and feeds the grade, ease, and online size guide each drop
revisit_triggers: a new pop-up batch shifts the observed fit or size distribution
the local sample is shown unrepresentative of the ship-to-California shopper

base.update_signal: the pop-up fitting data or its representativeness changes

nodes.definition: Derive the production size curve — the XS:S:M:L:XL:XXL ratio to manufacture — from the distribution of sizes actually sold at the pop-ups, because the right quantity per size is a demand fact, not a grade fact. The curve is UNKNOWN until the pop-ups run and is treated as a launch hypothesis; a wrong curve produces dead stock in the tails and stock-outs in the middle, both of which end in markdown that attacks the margin the A1 core carries. The curve sizes the dye-lot and CMT quantities per size and is distinct from the grade rule (how big each size is) it depends on.

included: the XS-XXL production ratio from sizes sold
the dead-stock/stock-out/markdown cost of a wrong curve
curve distinct from grade

pros.claim: Reading the manufacture ratio off real sizes sold avoids the markdown trap of a guessed curve
pros.example: producing to an observed 1:2:3:3:2:1 curve instead of an even split that strands XS/XXL and stocks out M/L

cons.claim: A curve fixed from early pop-up data can lock in a bias before the online population is known
cons.example: committing bulk to a youth-skewed local curve that misfits the broader ship-to-California size mix

failure_modes: splitting production evenly across sizes with no curve and stranding the tails
freezing the curve before enough fittings make it stable
acceptance_tests: the production XS-XXL ratio is derived from the distribution of sizes sold and is flagged UNKNOWN/hypothesis until the pop-ups run
revisit_triggers: the observed size distribution shifts across drops
online sales reveal a curve different from the local one

base.update_signal: the observed or online size distribution changes the production curve

nodes.definition: Validate the linear grade and the 5-6 inch ease against the local Central-Valley body population rather than assuming the national US sweater chart fits it. The ~46 percent-Hispanic Central-Valley distribution may not match the national chart, so the linear grade and the upper-band ease are launch hypotheses the in-person try-on confirms or breaks, including whether a non-linear grade break is needed at the XS or XXL extremes. This node consumes the pop-up fittings to either ratify the launch grade or trigger a grade revision before bulk commitment.

included: validating linear grade and ease on the local body
the possible non-linear break at XS/XXL
ratify-or-revise before bulk

cons.claim: Revising the grade on local data risks over-fitting to Turlock and misfitting the broader ship-to-California buyer

failure_modes: assuming the national chart fits and skipping local validation

nodes.definition: Use the offline fitting lab to buy down the online return rate, since online apparel returns run ~24 percent versus ~6 percent in-store and size is the #1 apparel return reason (the gap is robust even though the exact decimal is an estimate). Every offline fitting calibrates the online size guide so the ship-to-California shopper self-selects correctly, and returns are tracked by article and by size to find where the grade or guide is failing. Cutting size-driven returns directly protects contribution margin, the brand's stated kill-risk.

included: the ~24 vs ~6 percent return gap and size as #1 reason
calibrating the online size guide from offline fittings
returns split by article and size
excluded: the contribution-margin model owned by logistics

pros.claim: Calibrating the online size guide from real fittings cuts the size-driven returns that erode contribution margin
pros.example: publishing a 'measure your chest, compare to finished chest' guide built from pop-up data so online buyers stop ordering two sizes

cons.claim: A precise return figure is not this brand's number, so over-promising a return reduction can mislead planning
cons.example: quoting a 24 percent baseline as if measured for this line when only the online-vs-offline gap is robust

failure_modes: publishing a generic size guide not calibrated to the actual grade
tracking a blended return rate that hides which size or article is failing
acceptance_tests: the online size guide is calibrated from offline fittings and returns are tracked by article and size against the robust online-vs-offline gap
revisit_triggers: a return spike concentrated in one size or article

nodes.definition: Hold the binding honesty discipline across every numeric claim in the sizing system: ease bands, finished stitch density, per-fibre shrink allowances, return rates, and any price/MOQ/CAC/duty/throughput figure are labeled estimate-not-actual with method, basis, and confidence (the literal word estimate), or UNKNOWN where genuinely unknown, with a confirmation path (a PPS swatch, a wash test, the pop-up fittings, or a live quote). FACT anchors (US duties cotton ~16.5 percent / wool ~16 percent / acrylic ~32 percent; the standard knit grade increments) are citeable; off-paper mechanisms are described structurally, never as accusations, with amounts UNKNOWN. Coverage is a floor, not a ceiling.

included: estimate/UNKNOWN/FACT tagging with method and confidence
the confirmation path per estimate
duties and grade increments as FACT anchors

pros.claim: Tagging every figure estimate-not-actual with a confirmation path keeps the spec honest and tells the owner exactly what a swatch or pop-up must still confirm
pros.example: labeling the ~9 wales/in density and ~3-5 percent shrink as estimates pending the PPS swatch rather than asserting them as measured

cons.claim: Heavy labeling can read as hedging and slow a decision that a single swatch would resolve
cons.example: stacking estimate tags on a density that one wash-test would simply settle

failure_modes: stating a density, shrink, or return figure as fact without its confirmation path
faking precision on a duty, MOQ, or throughput band
acceptance_tests: every ease/density/shrink/return/price figure is tagged estimate-not-actual or UNKNOWN with method, confidence, and a confirmation path, and the FACT duty/increment anchors are cited
revisit_triggers: a PPS swatch, wash test, or pop-up replaces an estimate with a measured value

base.update_signal: a measured value replaces an estimate or a FACT anchor updates

nodes.definition: Assemble the consolidated sizing spec that turns the scattered measurement, grade, translation, and validation decisions into one tech-pack artifact: the finished-garment four-measurement M base, the linear grade table regenerated by the formula across XS-XXL, the integer wales/courses grade at the production density, the post-wash target with per-fibre offset, the per-point tolerances, the spirality/balanced-ply requirement, the labeled-estimate density and shrink figures with confirmation paths, and the placeholder for the pop-up-set size curve. It is the single artifact handed to the CAD programmer and the factory to knit and inspect against.

included: the integrated finished-spec + grade-table + stitch-grade + post-wash + tolerance tech pack
the size-curve placeholder
the hand-off to programmer and factory
excluded: the individual upstream decisions already made

pros.claim: One consolidated tech pack converts the grade math into an executable, inspectable artifact with no orphaned measurement
pros.example: a single sheet carrying the XS-XXL finished grade in inches and stitches, the post-wash target, and every tolerance that the programmer and QC both work from

cons.claim: A fixed tech pack can ossify and ignore a pop-up-driven grade revision if not paired with the review loop

failure_modes: a tech pack with a graded dimension missing its tolerance or stitch count
the size-curve placeholder left unfilled at bulk commitment
acceptance_tests: the tech pack lists every measurement with its finished value, formula-generated grade, integer stitch count, post-wash target, per-fibre offset, and tolerance, plus the size-curve placeholder

nodes.definition: Define the loop that keeps the sizing system alive: a per-drop review that takes the pop-up size curve and fit data and re-runs the grade, ease, and production ratio, plus material-change triggers — an online return spike concentrated in a size, a size-curve drift across drops, a PPS swatch showing a different shrink or density, a fibre or gauge change, a local-vs-online mismatch — that send the owner back through the grade formula and the local-body validation to re-plan. Without this loop the grade table and size curve silently drift out of alignment with the real body and the bulk quantities go wrong.

included: the per-drop pop-up-curve-to-grade review cadence
the material-change triggers
re-entry into the grade formula and local validation

pros.claim: A scheduled per-drop review catches grade drift and curve error before a bulk run commits to a stale size system
pros.example: a per-drop review that spots returns climbing at XXL and revises the grade or curve before the next order

cons.claim: Reviewing and re-grading too often churns the spec and prevents a stable size guide and curve from maturing
cons.example: re-grading every drop on noise so the online size guide never settles and buyers lose trust

failure_modes: no cadence set so the grade and curve are never revisited and drift

acceptance_tests: a per-drop review cadence and an explicit trigger list exist, each routing back to GRADE_FORMULA and LOCAL_BODY_VALIDATION
revisit_triggers: a material-change trigger fires

conflict_axes.name: finished_target_offset_vs_tight_tolerance

anti_rework_rules.rule: State the finished-vs-body rule and ease band before writing any measurement
anti_rework_rules.prevents: building a grade on body numbers and shipping every size off

anti_rework_rules.rule: Measure finished density on a washed swatch before translating inches to stitches
anti_rework_rules.prevents: handing the programmer a grade that does not resolve to integer wales/courses

anti_rework_rules.rule: Build to a post-wash target with the per-fibre offset before committing the stitch grade
anti_rework_rules.prevents: knitting to an off-machine dimension that washes down small

anti_rework_rules.rule: Attach a +/- tolerance to every measurement point when the grade is first written
anti_rework_rules.prevents: an unenforceable grade where on-average passes while garments drift off-size

anti_rework_rules.rule: Require balanced ply in the yarn PO before bulk knitting
anti_rework_rules.prevents: spiraled side seams that distort a correctly graded panel after wash

anti_rework_rules.rule: Label every density/shrink/return figure estimate-not-actual when first written
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a planning estimate being quoted downstream as a measured fact

anti_rework_rules.rule: Validate the linear grade and ease on the local body before bulk
anti_rework_rules.prevents: knitting a national-chart grade at scale that misfits the local population

anti_rework_rules.rule: Read the production size curve from pop-up sales before committing bulk quantities
anti_rework_rules.prevents: an even split that strands the tails and stocks out the middle into markdown

iteration_protocol.trigger: the fit intent, silhouette variant, or M-base measurement changes
iteration_protocol.action: re-fix the finished spec and re-run the grade formula and stitch translation

iteration_protocol.trigger: a PPS swatch shows a different finished density or residual shrinkage
iteration_protocol.action: re-translate inches to stitches and re-set the post-wash target and per-fibre offsets

iteration_protocol.trigger: online returns spike concentrated in a size or article
iteration_protocol.action: re-calibrate the size guide and re-validate the grade on the local body

iteration_protocol.trigger: a new pop-up batch shifts the observed fit or size distribution
iteration_protocol.action: update the size curve and re-validate the grade and ease

iteration_protocol.trigger: pop-up returns show a fit break at XS or XXL
iteration_protocol.action: extend the grade formula with a non-linear correction term and regenerate the table

iteration_protocol.trigger: a fibre blend ratio, gauge, or finishing route changes
iteration_protocol.action: re-check the gauge/grade/shrink coupling and the per-fibre offset and spirality control

priority_rationale: The finished-vs-body rule, the size set/block, and the four M-base measurements come first because every grade, translation, and tolerance depends on knowing the spec is finished-garment and what the base numbers are; the grade formula and the inch-to-stitch translation turn that base into a knittable, recomputable grade; the post-wash target, per-fibre offset, tolerance, spirality, and gauge/grade/shrink coupling make the grade producible and enforceable on real fabric; the pop-up fitting lab, size curve, local-body validation, and return reduction calibrate the grade against the real body and the production quantities; honesty labeling and the consolidated tech pack compose it into one honestly-labeled artifact; and the review loop comes last because it watches the whole spec and routes material changes back to the formula and the local validation.
